sourceCheck: RFC Editor records confirm that RFC 9110 (STD 97), RFC 9111 (STD 98) and RFC 9112 (STD 99) are Internet Standards published in June 2022, with no obsoleting RFCs. RFC 9110 and 9111 have no updating RFCs; RFC 9112 is updated only by RFC 9931, March 2026, whose protocol-change security considerations are outside this deck. Sources: [9110 metadata](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.json), [9111 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9111/), [9112 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9112/). RFC 9113 and 9114 are June 2022 Proposed Standards with no obsoleting or updating RFCs; RFC 9113 obsoletes RFC 7540 and 8740. Sources: [9113 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/), [9114 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9114/). RFC 6265 is an April 2011 Proposed Standard, and RFC 7838 is an April 2016 Proposed Standard; neither has an obsoleting or updating RFC listed. Sources: [6265 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6265/), [7838 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7838/). RFC 8297 was published as Experimental in December 2017, but its current status is Proposed Standard following an approved status change last updated 2025-02-05. Sources: [8297 record](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8297/), [status change](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/status-change-early-hints-to-proposed-standard/). RFC 10008 is a June 2026 Proposed Standard. RFC 9846 was published in July 2026 and obsoletes RFC 8446. Other checked supporting specifications are Proposed Standards: RFC 5789, 6585, 8246, 8470, 9000, 9204, 9213, 9218 and 9460; RFC 5861 is Informational. Verified errata found for RFC 9110: 7105, 7109, 7138, 7306, 7419 and 8268. These include the 308 method-preservation correction, the Accept quality-table correction, Range whitespace, the Accept-Charset reference correction and appendix corrections. The direct 9110 errata endpoint was unavailable, so the RFC Editor's informative inline-errata rendering was used for the audit, not as a card reference. RFC 9111 has no verified errata; 9004 and 9185 are Reported, 9166 is Held for Document Update, and 7695 is Rejected. RFC 6265 has verified errata 3444, 4148, 5518, 6093 and 7604; 6093 substitutes combine for fold, and 7604 scopes response-status processing to cookie-enabled user agents. Sources: [9110 errata rendering](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc9110.html), [9111 errata record](https://errata.rfc-editor.org/search/?rfc_number=9111), [6265 errata record](https://errata.rfc-editor.org/search/?rfc_number=6265). The cookie revision has not been published as an RFC: draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 remains an Active Internet-Draft dated 2025-12-01, in the RFC Editor queue and In Final Review. The queue XML endpoint was unavailable, so the received date was not independently confirmed. Source: [cookie revision record](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis/). The [Fetch Standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/) is a Living Standard displaying Last Updated 6 October 2026. MDN last-modified dates are September 23, 2026 for [Methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods), September 1, 2026 for [Set-Cookie](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie), and September 4, 2026 for [CORS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS). MDN lists QUERY, but its QUERY page's specification table says Unknown specification; QUERY cards therefore cite RFC 10008. MDN's [HTTP/2 glossary](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/HTTP_2) says server push has been removed from most major browser engines, while the RFC still defines it. The [HTTP/3 glossary](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/HTTP_3) broadly claims QUIC eliminates HTTP head-of-line blocking; the deck uses RFC 9114's narrower independent-stream-progress rule and accounts for QPACK dependencies. MDN's [Vary reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Vary) calls Vary: * uncacheable; RFC 9111 instead specifies that a stored response with that value always fails to match. MDN's Set-Cookie example gives /docs/Web/HTTP/ for /docs/Web/HTTP/index.html, whereas RFC 6265's default-path algorithm yields /docs/Web/HTTP. MDN's HTTP/1.x connection guide retains erroneous HTTP/1.0 persistence guidance involving retry-after and an outdated h2c Upgrade example; the relevant RFCs control. Other scope refinements: RFC 10008 defines range handling for QUERY, so a GET-only range assertion needs explicit RFC 9110 scope; ReadableStream bodies cause a CORS preflight for cross-origin requests, rather than same-origin requests; the Request constructor throws input errors while fetch() rejects with them; standalone Headers objects accept forbidden names, while request-guarded headers are sanitized. No other checked source invalidates the selected plan. Opened RFC Editor info pages for 9110, 9111, 9112, 9113, 9114, 6265, 7838, 8297, 10008, 9846, 9931, 5789, 6585, 5861, 8246, 8470, 9000, 9204, 9213, 9218 and 9460, using RFC Editor JSON metadata where an info page failed. Opened published RFC texts at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfcN.html for N = 9110, 9111, 9112, 9113, 9114, 9000, 9204, 6265, 7838, 10008, 5789, 6585, 5861, 8246, 8297, 8470, 9213, 9218 and 9460; .txt fallbacks were also opened for 7838, 5861, 8246, 8470 and 9213. Opened the requested errata endpoints, their available redirected records, the inline-errata renderings for 9110 and 6265, the cookie and Early Hints datatracker records, and the current RFC Editor queue page; rfc-index.xml and queue2.xml attempts failed. Opened Fetch and its HTTP-redirect section. Under https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/, opened Web/HTTP/Guides/Overview, Redirections, Content_negotiation, Conditional_requests, Range_requests, Caching, Cookies, Connection_management_in_HTTP_1.x, Evolution_of_HTTP and CORS; Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods and its GET, HEAD, DELETE, POST, PUT, PATCH, OPTIONS and QUERY pages; Web/HTTP/Reference/Status and its 100, 102, 103, 201, 202, 205, 300, 301, 302, 303, 307, 308, 400, 401, 404, 405, 409, 415, 422, 429, 502 and 504 pages; Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control, Vary, Set-Cookie, Alt-Svc, Origin and Access-Control-Max-Age; Glossary/HTTP_2, HTTP_3 and QUIC; Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch, Window/fetch, Request/Request, Response/ok, Response/statusText, Response/type and Headers/getSetCookie. The Accept-Charset reference attempt was unavailable, and the 102 page redirected to the status list.

cards.statement: A GET request has the same method semantics in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
cards.explanation: HTTP versions change how messages travel, while the shared method semantics retain their meaning.

cards.statement: A resource requires a new target URI when its representation changes.
cards.explanation: A target URI identifies a resource, whose representation can change over time. Updating that representation does not require a new URI.
cards.misconception: A URI identifies an immutable representation rather than a resource.

cards.statement: A client selects a proxy to forward its HTTP requests.
cards.explanation: The HTTP client chooses its proxy, possibly through configuration rules that select a proxy for particular requests.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client derives a response's status meaning from its reason phrase.
cards.explanation: The numeric status code carries a response's status meaning. A reason phrase is recommended text that may be replaced or omitted.
cards.misconception: The reason phrase determines how a client interprets the response status.

cards.statement: A recipient treats field names such as Content-Type and content-type as equivalent.
cards.explanation: Field names are case-insensitive, so different capitalization identifies the same field.

cards.statement: A recipient may combine repeated list-field lines into a comma-separated value in their received order.
cards.explanation: A recipient may combine list-field values with commas while preserving their received order; that order can affect interpretation.

cards.statement: A sender can use two Content-Type field lines to describe two possible media types for one message.
cards.explanation: Content-Type has single-value syntax. A sender must not repeat it to supply a list of alternative media types.
cards.misconception: Repeated field lines let a sender turn a single-valued field into a list.

source.title: RFC 9110 §5.3: Sender Restrictions on Repeated Fields

cards.statement: A proxy forwards unknown fields unless Connection or explicit configuration calls for other handling.
cards.explanation: A proxy must forward unrecognized fields, subject to Connection handling and explicit configuration that blocks or transforms them.

cards.statement: A server silently ignores request fields that exceed the size it is willing to process.
cards.explanation: A server must answer oversized request fields with an appropriate 4xx response when they exceed what it wishes to process.
cards.misconception: A server may discard oversized request fields and continue processing the request.

cards.statement: An intermediary may discard trailer fields while forwarding an HTTP message.
cards.explanation: Intermediaries can discard trailers in transit, so a server should keep information essential to the user agent out of them.

cards.statement: A client distinguishes http and https target URIs by the letter case of their host names.
cards.explanation: The host component of an http or https URI is case-insensitive. Changing its capitalization does not identify a different target.
cards.misconception: Host names in HTTP URIs are case-sensitive.

cards.statement: A sender should put a username and password in an https target URI to supply credentials.
cards.explanation: User:password userinfo is deprecated. A sender must not generate userinfo in an http or https target URI within an HTTP message.
cards.misconception: Embedding user:password in a target URI is a recommended HTTP authentication mechanism.

cards.statement: An origin server's incidental logging is compatible with safe request method semantics.
cards.explanation: Safety concerns the action the client requests. A server's incidental logging does not make a safe request unsafe.

cards.statement: A client classifies DELETE as non-idempotent when repeating it produces a different status code.
cards.explanation: DELETE remains idempotent when repeated requests yield different responses. Idempotence concerns the intended server effect, rather than identical status codes.
cards.misconception: Idempotent requests produce identical response status codes when repeated.

cards.statement: A proxy may retry a non-idempotent request automatically after the connection fails.
cards.explanation: A proxy must not automatically retry a non-idempotent request, including after a connection failure.
cards.misconception: A connection failure permits a proxy to replay a non-idempotent request automatically.

cards.statement: A server answering HEAD should send the header fields it would send for GET.
cards.explanation: A HEAD response should match GET's header fields. A server may omit fields whose values are determined only while generating content.

cards.statement: An origin server interprets GET request content as a standardized filter for the selected representation.
cards.explanation: GET request content has no generally defined semantics. HTTP does not standardize using it to filter the selected representation.
cards.misconception: HTTP defines GET request content as a query filter.

cards.statement: An origin server sends 201 when a successful PUT creates the target resource's first representation.
cards.explanation: A successful PUT that creates the target resource's first representation requires a 201 response.

cards.statement: A cache uses explicit freshness alone to establish the cacheability of a POST response.
cards.explanation: A cacheable POST response needs explicit freshness and Content-Location equal to the POST's target URI.
cards.misconception: Explicit freshness is sufficient to make a POST response cacheable.

cards.statement: A server sends an ETag in a successful PUT response even after transforming the submitted content.
cards.explanation: A successful PUT response must omit validators if the server transformed the submitted content before saving it.
cards.misconception: A server may return a validator for transformed content in a successful PUT response.

cards.statement: An origin server includes Allow in a 405 response to list the resource's supported methods.
cards.explanation: A 405 response must include Allow. The field identifies the methods the target resource currently supports.

cards.statement: PATCH has idempotent method semantics for a resource's partial updates.
cards.explanation: PATCH is not idempotent by definition. An individual patch can still be designed so repetition has the same intended effect.
cards.misconception: Partial updates make PATCH inherently idempotent.

cards.statement: QUERY is a safe method even though its request content carries the query.
cards.explanation: QUERY defines safe retrieval using request content to express the query; the client does not request a state change to the target resource.

cards.statement: A client uses an asterisk target in OPTIONS to ask about the server's general communication options.
cards.explanation: OPTIONS with an asterisk target concerns the server in general, rather than a particular target resource.

cards.statement: A client interprets an unrecognized 4xx status code as 400.
cards.explanation: A client must treat an unfamiliar status code as the x00 code of its class; an unfamiliar 4xx therefore has 400 semantics.

cards.statement: A client treats 100 Continue as the final response to its request.
cards.explanation: 100 Continue is an interim response. The client still waits for a final response to learn the request's outcome.
cards.misconception: Permission to continue sending a request also establishes its final outcome.

cards.statement: A server's Location field in a 201 response identifies the primary resource created.
cards.explanation: When a 201 response includes Location, that field identifies the primary resource created by the request.

cards.statement: A server's 202 response confirms that processing the requested action succeeds.
cards.explanation: 202 means the server accepted the request for processing. Processing remains incomplete and the eventual outcome is uncertain.
cards.misconception: Acceptance for processing guarantees successful completion.

cards.statement: A server includes updated form content in a 205 Reset Content response.
cards.explanation: A server must not generate content in a 205 response. The response asks the user agent to reset the view used to submit the request.
cards.misconception: 205 supplies replacement content for the form the user agent should reset.

cards.statement: An origin server includes WWW-Authenticate in a 401 response.
cards.explanation: A server generating 401 must include a WWW-Authenticate challenge applicable to the target resource.

cards.statement: A server's 404 response tells the client that the resource's absence is permanent.
cards.explanation: 404 leaves the duration of the resource's absence unspecified; it does not establish that the absence is permanent.
cards.misconception: 404 establishes that a resource is permanently absent.

cards.statement: A server's 409 response indicates a conflict with the target resource's current state.
cards.explanation: 409 reports a conflict between the request and the target resource's current state, which the user might resolve before resubmitting.

cards.statement: A server uses 415 for unsupported formats it discovers by inspecting request content.
cards.explanation: A server can discover an unsupported format by examining the request data itself, rather than relying on its declared Content-Type.

cards.statement: A server can use 422 Unprocessable Content for a request whose content has malformed syntax.
cards.explanation: 422 concerns content with valid syntax and an understood content type whose instructions the server cannot process.
cards.misconception: 422 reports malformed content syntax rather than unprocessable instructions.

cards.statement: A server's 429 response may include Retry-After to suggest a delay before another request.
cards.explanation: A 429 response may include Retry-After to advise when the client should try again; the field is optional.

cards.statement: A gateway uses 502 Bad Gateway when an upstream server fails to answer within the allotted time.
cards.explanation: An upstream timeout calls for 504 Gateway Timeout. A 502 reports an invalid response from an upstream server.
cards.misconception: 502 represents an upstream timeout rather than an invalid upstream response.

cards.statement: A 301 response tells a user agent to treat the new URI as a temporary replacement.
cards.explanation: 301 identifies a permanent URI replacement, so future references ought to use the new URI.
cards.misconception: 301 communicates a temporary move to another URI.

cards.statement: A user agent preserves the request method when it automatically follows a 307 redirect.
cards.explanation: A user agent must retain the request method when automatically following a 307 response.

cards.statement: A server's 303 response presents Location as an equivalent URI for the target resource.
cards.explanation: A 303 points to a resource supplying an indirect response. Its Location URI is not considered equivalent to the original target URI.
cards.misconception: 303 declares the redirect destination equivalent to the original target URI.

cards.statement: A cache classifies 308 Permanent Redirect as heuristically cacheable.
cards.explanation: 308 is heuristically cacheable, subject to the request method and explicit cache controls.

cards.statement: A user agent resolves a relative Location value against the request's target URI.
cards.explanation: The user agent resolves a relative redirect Location against the request's target URI to obtain the destination.

cards.statement: A user agent discards the old fragment when Location omits a fragment in a redirect.
cards.explanation: A redirect Location with no fragment inherits the fragment, if any, of the original URI reference used to generate the target URI.
cards.misconception: Omitting a fragment from Location clears the original URI reference's fragment.

cards.statement: A server's 300 response offers representations for the user agent to choose between.
cards.explanation: 300 offers alternatives so the user agent or user can select a preferred representation.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser preserves Authorization when a redirect reaches another origin.
cards.explanation: HTTP-redirect fetch removes Authorization once the redirect reaches an origin different from the request's current origin.
cards.misconception: Authorization follows a fetch() redirect across origins unchanged.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser changes a POST request to GET when following a 302 redirect.
cards.explanation: For a 302 response to POST, HTTP-redirect fetch changes the method to GET.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser keeps request-body headers when a redirect changes the method to GET.
cards.explanation: When HTTP-redirect fetch changes a method to GET, it deletes request-body headers such as Content-Type.
cards.misconception: Request-body metadata survives a redirect that rewrites the method to GET.

cards.statement: A user agent changes QUERY to GET when it follows a 301 redirect.
cards.explanation: QUERY retains its method on a 301 redirect. The historical POST-to-GET exception does not apply to QUERY.
cards.misconception: 301 applies the historical POST method-rewriting exception to QUERY.

cards.statement: MDN says browsers execute HTTP redirects before HTML redirects.
cards.explanation: MDN places HTTP redirects first because they occur before the browser receives the page that could trigger them.
cards.volatilityNote: This card follows MDN's description of browser redirect precedence, which browser behavior or documentation could change.
